_comment: The yardstick. One entry per capture in ../captures/manifest.json, and every facet a capture is scored on is named EXPLICITLY here — there is no aggregate number and no facet a reader has to infer. A facet a capture's entry does not name is not scored for that capture and does not enter that facet's denominator.

_facets.status: the terminal queue status: filed | needs_input | triage | rejected | failed
_facets.reason: for a `rejected` status, the report's own reason_code (capture.schema.REJECTION_REASONS)
_facets.type: the `type:` frontmatter of the page that actually landed, read back out of git
_facets.folder: the directory the page landed in
_facets.anchor: {kind: entity|company, ids: [registry id, ...]} — read from the filed page's server-stamped `entity:` frontmatter, so it is the resolved REGISTRY ID and never the agent's spelling. `company` means the page filed with an empty `entity:` list, which is what a company-wide anchoring outcome stamps.
_facets.edits: paths of pages OTHER than the filed one that this commit changed — what edits.apply_declared actually performed from the agent's declaration. Scored by CONTAINMENT (run_filing._edits_match): every path named here has to be among them, and a further edit does not fail the facet — the gates confine a declared edit to additive growth on an existing in-lane page, so an extra one is harmless by construction, while the throwaway repo grows during the run and a later capture may legitimately backlink a page an earlier one created. A capture that owes no edit therefore names NO `edits` key: an empty list would be true for every backend and still fill the denominator.
_facets.attempts: how many times the agent was called for this capture (counted at the Deps.agent seam, not read from any report)
_facets.bounces: corrective retries = max(0, attempts - 1); one bounce means the first pass was vetoed and the agent got its single corrective pass
_facets.park_question: for a park: the unresolved name(s) the question captured, matched loosely
_facets.decisions: for a meeting: one entry per decision page, paired one-to-one and greedily in the order written. An entry asserts its own ANCHOR (exact — a resolved registry id, or the empty list a company-wide outcome stamps) and MAY assert a title (matched loosely — see the runner and _morphology). The anchor is the load-bearing pair-er and the title is optional because that is what five measured runs showed: across three distinct brittleness shapes the anchors were right every time while the titles were stable only in a proper noun or a term the transcript itself repeats. So a title is written where it HELD across runs and omitted where the distiller could defensibly put the word on the sibling decision — omitting it moves the assertion off the model's vocabulary and onto its judgment, which is what this facet is for. An entry asserting neither is refused by _check_set (it would match whatever page is left), and a title-less entry must be written LAST because it is the weakest matcher.
_facets.reuse: for a meeting re-filed after a park: whether the decisions the parked pass distilled survived the re-file

_looseness: Titles are matched on normalized words, never literally: an expected title matches a page when every significant word of the expectation appears in the page's own path, in either grammatical number (see _morphology). evals/README.md records what a literal-word expectation cost the QA golden (`globex-meeting-budget`); this set does not repeat it. Everything else — status, ids, folders, counts — is exact, because those are facts with one spelling.
_morphology: An expected title is written in UNINFLECTED content words — a proper noun plus a stable noun — and never in the verb form one run happened to produce. run_filing._words does no stemming and deliberately will not grow any (a stem table is a second yardstick nobody reviews), so `tracked` and `tracking` are still two different words and an expectation naming one of them scores the model's grammar. EXACTLY ONE fold is made, at the comparison rather than in the tokenizer (run_filing._same_word): a trailing `s`, in either direction, so `review` and `reviews` are one word. It was added on MEASUREMENT, not on taste — three independent runs of the same code on the same model titled F08's review decision two ways, singular twice (PASS) and plural once (FAIL), with the anchors right every time, so a 2-denominator facet was flipping on grammatical number. A plural written `es` is still not folded (`process`/`processes` misses), which is the measure of how narrow this is. The fold is ONE-DIRECTIONAL — the predicate is strictly weaker than the one it replaces, so a recorded PASS cannot become a FAIL and only a FAIL can flip; that is what keeps every score already in evals/history.ndjson comparable without a re-run. Where two expected decisions could both match one page, the MORE SPECIFIC one is written first: matching is greedy and one-to-one, so the narrow expectation has to claim its page before the broad one takes it — and that pairing is the one place a weaker predicate could still re-bind and cost a PASS, which is why tests/evals/test_filing_golden_fixture.py::test_no_expected_decision_title_can_swallow_a_later_ones_page calls the same matcher and so widened its own net with it.
_fixture_narration: These expectations, and PROVENANCE.json beside the mini repo, are where the reasoning about the MEASUREMENT lives — never in the fixture pages themselves. The agent under measurement reads those pages while it files, so a page explaining which facet it exists to probe is a page telling the model the answer, and a score measured that way is not a score. The pages read as ordinary knowledge a colleague wrote; every `why` below says what that page is doing for the instrument.

expectations.why: The base case: ordinary prose about a registered entity, filed as a note. If this one moves, nothing else in the set is interpretable. It names NO `edits` expectation, and that silence is a correction the first Sonnet-5 baseline earned before a single number was recorded: this entry used to pin `edits: []`, and the run declared a reciprocal `related:` link on `wiki/notes/Northwind Freight Onboarding.md` — which is correct filing, because this material CONTINUES that page's account (it is the depot rollout status, and it names the two depots that went first). The empty list asserted an assumption about how one backend would file, not anything the brief requires, so scoring it would have marked correct cross-linking down: the `globex-meeting-budget` lesson, caught this time while the fixture could still be edited. Where a declared edit IS a requirement is F03.

A capture about an organization the registry does not know MUST park and ask, not guess and not fall back to company-wide scope. Then the ask-back loop: a reply that resolves must file the capture anchored to the registry's own entity.
expectations.reply: Halcyon Grid is our internal working name for the Northwind Freight pilot — file it under Northwind Freight.

expectations.why: The material answers the weekend-cover question `wiki/notes/Northwind Freight Onboarding.md` left open, so that page is owed a reciprocal link. The agent may not write it — it declares the edit and edits.apply_declared performs it — so this facet scores whether the backend RECOGNISED the debt, which is judgment, not mechanism. Two properties of the target page are load-bearing and neither is stated on it: it existed before this capture arrived (an additive edit to an EXISTING page is only a real claim against a page nobody created in the same commit), and it records the open question without answering it, so the continuation is genuine rather than arbitrary. The same material also substantially covers ground that page already covers — a backend that files a second page and says nothing about the first has quietly duplicated the corpus. The list stays at one path under containment scoring: it is the edit that is OWED, and the first Sonnet-5 baseline declared two more beside it — a policy page, and the page F01 had filed minutes earlier in the same throwaway repo — neither of which a yardstick written against the frozen fixture could have named, and both of which the gates had already confined to additive growth.

Byte-identical material to F01 from a different person: already in the graph, so it is refused with a pointer rather than filed a second time. Deterministic and pre-agent — this facet is the one that must NOT move between backends, and a change here means the dedup levels moved, not the model.

A decision that genuinely belongs to no entity. The failure this watches for is the tempting one: anchoring it to whichever organization the corpus talks about most, because an anchored page files and a company-wide one needs a written reason.
Material whose subject is a term rather than an event — the third creatable type, and the one a backend under pressure downgrades to a note.

Sixteen figures in one capture, one of them explicitly provisional. No gate re-checks figures at filing time (ADR 026 D2), so what this scores is the surrounding judgment — right entity, right type, filed in one pass rather than bounced. It anchors to the entity every other capture ignores, which keeps its anchoring judgment independent of the one the corpus talks about most; and no page in the mini repo carries a figure of its own, so a number that appears on the filed page can only have come from this capture.

The meeting flow's own shape: a source page, a meeting page and one decision page per decision — with each decision anchoring INDEPENDENTLY. One of these two belongs to an entity and the other to nobody, which is the property a single-anchor implementation cannot express and a single-decision transcript cannot reveal. The second title is the single word `review` on purpose: the transcript decides 'one shared list of what every review has to cover', so `checklist` (the thing being REPLACED, named once in passing), `shared`, `scope` and `standardise` are each one plausible paraphrase away from absent, and an expectation naming one of them would score the distiller's wording. The anchors carry the discrimination here — this decision is the company-wide one and its sibling is not.

A transcript whose subject is not in the registry parks the WHOLE capture in one ask naming every unresolved name — a partial page set is worse than an honest park. Then the reply resolves it and the set files. The `reuse` facet asks the question that matters after a park: did the capture LOSE a decision on the way back? The two decisions are 'Wren gets tracked formally under Quillon Labs' and 'the weekly summary joins the shared one', and they are paired on ANCHOR rather than on prose. This capture is where the third distinct title brittleness was measured: the expectation used to be `Wren summary` + `Wren`, and Sonnet titled the same two decisions `project-wren-tracked-formally-under-quillon-labs` + `weekly-summaries-consolidated-into-the-shared-summary`, putting the word `summary` on the OTHER decision than the yardstick assumed. Both splits are defensible readings of one transcript; which noun lands on which page is the distiller's prose, not its judgment. What to assert instead was settled by re-scoring all SEVEN recorded runs of this phase rather than by reading the newest one, and the answer inverted the assumption that the anchor is always the stable half. The TRACKING decision is stable in both: `quillon-labs` in 7/7 and the words `project wren` in 7/7. The SUMMARY decision is stable only in its TITLE — `shared`, `summary` and `weekly` in 7/7 — while its anchor is `quillon-labs` in six runs and company-wide in one, so asserting the anchor there would pin the yardstick to a single sample and score six correct runs a miss. So: entry one asserts the bare word `summary`, which appears on the summary page in every run and on the tracking page in none, and asserts NO anchor; entry two asserts `Wren` plus the entity anchor, which is the fact this whole ask-back capture exists to prove. `summary` is written FIRST because it is the narrow one — `Wren` appears in BOTH titles in six of the seven runs, so it is the broad matcher and the specific-first rule puts it second.
expectations.reply: Project Wren is the internal codename for the Quillon Labs collaboration — file it under Quillon Labs.

expectations.why: The sharpest anchoring probe in the set. The material names two registered entities and is plainly about only one of them; the other appears in a single sentence that says so explicitly. A backend that anchors on mention frequency, on first mention, or on whichever entity the corpus knows best gets this wrong — and gets everything else in this set right, which is exactly the gradual degradation the instrument exists to catch.

The first of four captures added for issue #77, where entity resolution stopped being a suffix list in Python and became the agent's judgment fenced by code. This one is the case the suffix list NEVER had: the material consistently writes a group form of a registered name that `normalize` does not fold and never did, so no deterministic path resolves it in either direction. What DOES reach the agent is the registered entity itself, because whole-token containment already surfaces it — the material's token run carries the registered spelling inside it. So this measures judgment with the candidate already in hand: does the agent read a qualifier as the same company, and does it say so. Substantively unambiguous on purpose (depots, site access, a standing maintenance contract — the entity page's own subject matter), because an instrument whose fixture is genuinely ambiguous measures the ambiguity.

The ABBREVIATION direction, and the only case in the set that no wording in any skill could have fixed. The material writes the short house form and never the registered one, so whole-token containment of the REGISTRY spelling inside the material finds nothing: before `gather._entities` learned to match a distinctive sub-run of a registered name, this candidate never reached the agent at all and the capture could only park. The corpus evidence is on the entity's own page, phrased as the ordinary fact it is — nearly nobody writes the full name — exactly as the research partner's page has always recorded its own short form. Two things are being measured together here, which is deliberate: that the near miss is SURFACED (platform) and that it is JUDGED rather than guessed (agent).

The benign twin, and it matters MORE now that resolution is a judgment: the failure mode of an agentic resolver is a confident wrong answer, so this belongs here and not only in a unit test. Two registered entities share a prefix and are genuinely different organizations — an independent legal practice and a maintenance contractor, no ownership, no shared work — and BOTH are handed to the agent, because the material's token run carries the shorter registered name inside the longer one. The capture is about the practice alone and must anchor to it alone. A run that anchors this to the contractor, or to both, has merged two identities, and every page filed against the wrong one is a timeline nobody will re-read. The distinctness is written on both entity pages as ordinary knowledge — a real brain would hold exactly that fact, because a real brain's people confuse the two names too.

The regression guard for the judgment that MOVED. `Registry.canonical_id` used to fold a legal-form suffix, so this spelling resolved mechanically; it no longer does (`kernel.normalize` splits the resolution key from the mint gate's collision key), and the point of this capture is that the OUTCOME must not change even though the decider did. If moving judgment out of code lost behaviour, this is the cell that goes red, and it goes red for the whole class rather than for one spelling. Written as an ordinary operational note about a name mismatch on a certificate, not as a puzzle about names: the material's own subject happens to be the same confusion the resolver is being asked to see through, which is how the confusion actually shows up in a real brain.
